Where do the month names come from?
January is named after Janus, the Roman god of doors and beginnings.
February comes from Februa, a Roman festival of purification.
March is named after Mars, the Roman god of war.
April probably comes from Latin aperire, “to open”, as buds open in spring.
May is named after Maia, a Roman goddess of growth.
June is named after Juno, queen of the Roman gods.
July is named after Julius Caesar.
August is named after the Roman emperor Augustus.
September comes from Latin septem, “seven”: it was the seventh month of the old Roman calendar.

Easter, Christmas and other Christian feasts, with Western and Orthodox dates.

Western churches calculate Easter with the Gregorian calendar, Orthodox churches with the Julian calendar; all dates are shown on the Gregorian calendar. Some Orthodox churches keep the fixed feasts, Christmas included, 13 days later on the Julian calendar.
Jewish holidays and the Hebrew date: Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur, Hanukkah, Passover and more.

Jewish days begin at sunset the evening before; holidays are shown on their first full day, and the Hebrew date follows the daytime. Durations follow the Diaspora: in Israel Passover lasts 7 days, Shavuot 1 day, and Simchat Torah falls on Shemini Atzeret. Dates are calculated with the rules of the Hebrew calendar.
The Solar Hijri calendar: months and years of the solar year, with Nowruz, Sizdah Bedar, Yalda Night and other Iranian cultural days.

The year begins on the day of the March equinox if it falls before noon Tehran time (UTC+3:30), otherwise on the next day; dates here are calculated by this rule. Months are shown with their Iranian names; in Afghanistan the months take zodiac names (Hamal, Sawr…). Chaharshanbe Suri is held on the Tuesday evening before the last Wednesday of the year and Yalda Night on the last evening of Azar; Mehregan falls on 16 Mehr in the old Zoroastrian count. Religious and political commemorations are not shown.

Month starts and solar terms are calculated astronomically for China time (UTC+8). The Korean and Vietnamese lunar calendars are separate calendars because some months begin one day earlier or later there.

The Ethiopian date and Ethiopian holidays such as Enkutatash, Meskel, Genna, Timkat and Fasika.

The Ethiopian year has twelve 30-day months and Pagume of 5 or 6 days; it begins on 11 September (12 September in the year before a Gregorian leap year) and runs 7–8 years behind the Gregorian year. Feasts follow the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church: Genna falls on 7 January every year and Fasika on Orthodox Easter.
The Coptic date and the feasts of the Coptic Orthodox Church: Nayrouz, Christmas, Epiphany and Easter.

Coptic years count from the Era of the Martyrs (AD 284); the months begin on the same days as in the Ethiopian calendar, and the year starts on 11 September (12 September in the year before a Gregorian leap year). Christmas is kept on 29 Koiak, or 28 Koiak in the year after a leap year, so it always falls on 7 January; Easter follows the Orthodox reckoning.

How far along is the season?

Earth travels once around the Sun every year. But it doesn\'t stand up straight: its axis is tilted 23.4 degrees, always the same way. For half the year the northern half leans toward the Sun and it\'s summer; for the other half it leans away and it\'s winter.
A common mix-up: seasons don\'t happen because we get closer to or farther from the Sun. Earth is closest to the Sun in early January – right in our winter!

In summer the Sun is high in the sky; its rays hit the ground straight on and warm a small patch well. In winter the Sun is low; the same light spreads over a bigger area and warms it less. Winter days are also short, so the ground has less time to warm up.
Does winter start on December 1 or December 21?

Both are right, because there are two ways to count. Astronomers start a season by the Sun\'s position: winter begins on the longest night (December 21, the winter solstice). Meteorologists (weather scientists) use whole months to keep their numbers simple: December, January and February are winter. That\'s why some calendars say “winter starts on December 1”.
Flipped on the other half of the world
While we have winter, it\'s summer in Australia, South Africa and Argentina. Kids there often celebrate New Year on the beach!
June 21 is the longest day of the year and December 21 the longest night (in the northern half).
On the equinoxes in March and September, day and night are almost equal.
At the North Pole the Sun doesn\'t set for months in summer, and doesn\'t rise for months in winter.
Near the equator summer and winter feel almost the same; instead there are rainy and dry seasons.
In the northern half, summer is a few days longer than winter: Earth moves a little slower when it\'s farther from the Sun.

The cloud forecast covers today and the next 6 days.

We use the low, mid and high cloud cover and the precipitation for the hour closest to sunrise and sunset (Open-Meteo). Rain of 0.5 mm per hour or more, or low cloud of %1$s or more: Poor. Low cloud below %2$s and mid or high cloud between %3$s and %4$s: Good; these clouds catch the colours of the light. Low cloud below %5$s: Fair (a clear sky also falls here: clean but plain). Anything else: Poor. This is a forecast; clouds can change within a few hours.

Direction is given in degrees clockwise from north: 90° east, 180° south, 270° west. Where the sun rises and sets shifts with the seasons; in the northern hemisphere it moves north in summer and south in winter. You can plan your framing and spot in advance.
